title: America's Treasury Secretary Threatens Allies with Divine Wrath, Proving He Has No Cards
dek: Treasury Secretary Bessent portrays America as an angry god, demanding allies submit as if to Pascal's wager. Farrell sees through the editorial: the louder the threat, the clearer it is that America lacks the means to follow through, and allies are already hedging.
why: A contrarian reading of a seemingly tough Treasury editorial: theological threats rarely materialize, and understanding this helps predict allies' true leverage in trade negotiations.
who: Decision-makers in cross-border business, investors watching dollar assets and tariff risks, and policy researchers trying to gauge whether allies will cave.
skip: Skip the first 4 minutes of intro and subscription pitch, and start directly with Carney's speech and Bessent's editorial.

points.h: The Treasury chief casts America as an angry god
points.body: In Bessent's Financial Times editorial on 'economic D-Day,' he frames allies' choice as a Pascal's wager. Farrell's read: he's essentially saying you must treat America as God, appeasing this wrathful deity by all means, lest it strike you with lightning. Farrell likens it to a 17th-century Puritan sermon, which could be titled 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God,' except the sinners are the rest of the world. The problem is that such pulpit-thumping usually signals a pastor losing his congregation, not strength.

points.h: The louder the shout, the softer the stick
points.body: Roosevelt's maxim was 'speak softly and carry a big stick.' Farrell says Bessent reverses it: speak bigly and carry a soft stick. The real test is China: it is currently the country most capable of supporting Iran, and Bessent avoids answering whether America would dare to bring its wrath down on China if it continues buying Iranian oil. Farrell believes markets and nations are betting 'no.' So the editorial reads as an empty threat—the more it overpromises, the more it reveals America bluffing at an empty table.

points.h: Flexible realism equals no strategy at all
points.body: Using 'flexible realism' to explain White House behavior is throwing a blanket over chaos. Farrell says the term, unpacked, means only: America does whatever it wants, and other countries should adapt. What actually drives the White House is not strategy but a scramble for attention, like Cosimo de' Medici making everyone revolve around him—but Trump does 'a stupid version': to be the center of attention, he'll make decisions that are extremely foolish in both the long and short term. Other countries' response, therefore, is to cut losses rather than keep betting.

Federalist Paper No. 10 offered 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition': let each person's drive for power cancel out the others, grinding toward an equilibrium close to the public interest. Farrell says this mechanism has been dismantled from both ends. One end is the Republican Party: internal dissent has nearly vanished; senators won't openly block even if they object; same-party control of all three branches short-circuits the original checks. The other end is the federal bureaucracy: the Supreme Court embraces the 'unitary executive' theory, inspectors general are fired or intimidated, and ordinary civil servants are converted to at-will employees. A fundamentally incompetent person sits atop the system, and errors amplify into national madness.

points.h: Rebuilding US institutions requires learning to experiment
points.body: Farrell doesn't think institutions can return to the old consensus of the early 1990s to 2015, but he also doesn't see America doomed to disaster. His hopeful example is New York Mayor Mamdani's experiment: building feedback loops between city government and the public, turning people's real troubles into policy, and using social media to show citizens 'I'm listening and acting.' He explicitly links this style to Roosevelt's 'bold, persistent experimentation': keep what works, discard what doesn't. The open question is whether America's media and political system can tolerate a politician openly saying 'this path didn't work, let's try another'—without that tolerance, experiments won't go far.

points.h: The more flexible, the less anyone takes you seriously
points.body: The biggest problem with flexible realism is that it destroys an asset that is depleted by caprice—credibility. Farrell cites Nobel laureate Thomas Schelling: one of a nation's most important assets is credibility; promises and threats that can be carried out are what actually work in negotiations. If you change your mind at will, and threats made yesterday vanish today, eventually no one takes you seriously. Farrell sees America in that state today: other nations still fear its capacity to harm, but no longer believe in its capacity for long-term action. His image: a drunk grandfather with a shotgun, and everyone just humors him so he doesn't fire.

points.h: America is smashing its own web with a sledgehammer
points.body: The core argument of Farrell and Newman's 'Underground Empire' is that globalization is a web of interdependence—supply chains stitched together by thousands of suppliers across dozens of countries, with dollar clearing as the nervous system. America built this system with one hand and reserved a 'house advantage' with the other, using the threat of cutting off the network to discipline others. The Trump administration's approach is not a surgical dismantling but swinging a sledgehammer semi-randomly at various parts. Farrell's direction is clear: full decoupling would be a disaster; the option for nations is not independence but making interdependence resilient, while major powers relearn the language of 'restraint.'

points.h: A rare-earth card punctures the myth of inevitable victory
points.body: On last year's 'Liberation Day' for tariffs, Bessent publicly said America held all the aces and China had no cards. Weeks later, China played its rare-earth and critical-minerals card, and America suddenly realized it held a busted flush—a hand that looked fierce but never materialized. Farrell sees this as the moment that sobered the US side; since then, speeches by Marco Rubio and others reflect the recognition that China can materially harm the US economy. The US and China now live in a fragile balance where each knows 'I can hurt you badly,' but they have not yet sat down to turn that balance into more stable rules.

terms.def: God's existence cannot be proven, but believing yields higher expected value; Bessent twists it into 'submitting to America is safer.'
